items.body:
## Summary

After updating Hermes Agent, the desktop UI can appear to lose all previous conversations on both macOS and Windows. The conversations are not deleted: the session database remains intact, but the session-list API fails because the updated code queries a column that has not been added to the existing database yet.

## Environment

- macOS (Apple Silicon), Hermes 0.20.0 desktop build
- Hermes checkout/build commit: `69bedb7be` (`fix(desktop): stop reporting false failure on successful backend updates`)
- The same symptom has also occurred on Windows (no Windows log attached yet).
- Default data directory: `~/.hermes` (`%USERPROFILE%\\.hermes` on Windows)
- Canonical history database: `~/.hermes/state.db`

## Evidence

On macOS, immediately after the update, the GUI log repeatedly reported:

```text
GET /api/sessions failed
sqlite3.OperationalError: no such column: s.last_activity_at
```

The database was on schema v23 while the updated session-list code expected the v25 activity columns. The web endpoint appears to open a read-only connection and fails before the normal writable migration path runs.

Running the normal CLI command `hermes sessions list` migrated the database to schema v25. After restarting the desktop app:

- all 57 sessions and 3,248 messages were still present;
- SQLite `PRAGMA integrity_check` returned `ok`;
- the history could be listed again.

This indicates a migration-order/listing failure rather than data deletion.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use Hermes with an existing `state.db` from the previous schema.
2. Update Hermes to a build whose session list reads `last_activity_at`.
3. Start the desktop app immediately after the update.
4. Open the conversation history/sidebar.
5. The session-list request fails and previous conversations appear to be missing.
6. Run `hermes sessions list`, restart the app, and the history returns.

## Expected behavior

The updater or backend should migrate `state.db` before starting the updated desktop/web session-list code. If migration cannot run, the UI should show an explicit recovery error instead of an empty history.

## Actual behavior

The update completes, but the history UI appears empty because `GET /api/sessions` crashes with a missing-column error.

## Temporary workaround

Run:

```bash
hermes sessions list
```

Then restart Hermes. On Windows, run the equivalent command from the Hermes installation.

Could the update flow make the migration ordering safe on both platforms, and add a regression test for upgrading an existing schema v23 database to v25?

items.title: bug(persistence): update_session_model() doesn't persist provider in model_config → cross-provider fallback sessions 404 on resume

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Bug Description

When a session falls back from the primary model (e.g. `nvidia/z-ai/glm-5.2`) to a fallback model on a **different provider** (e.g. `custom:opencode-zen/deepseek-v4-flash-free`), and the user then switches to that fallback model with `/model` (or via the Hermes Desktop model selector), the session persists only the **model name** in `state.db` — not its **provider**. On the next session resume, the runtime recombines the persisted model with the **primary provider from `config.yaml`** (which doesn't serve that model), producing a guaranteed `404 page not found` on every turn.

This is distinct from the runtime credential-pool desync tracked in #56885 and #15743 — those occur *within* a live session. This bug is a **persistence gap**: `update_session_model()` writes the model name to the `sessions.model` column but never writes `model` or `provider` keys into the `model_config` JSON blob, so the provider/model pair is lost across restarts.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a primary model on one provider and a fallback model on a **different** provider:
   ```yaml
   model:
     provider: nvidia
     default: z-ai/glm-5.2
   
   fallback_providers:
     - provider: custom:opencode-zen
       model: deepseek-v4-flash-free
   ```

2. Start a session (CLI or gateway). The primary model works: `provider=nvidia model=z-ai/glm-5.2`.

3. Trigger a fallback — either let the primary rate-limit/fail, or use `/model` to switch to `deepseek-v4-flash-free`. The fallback works: `provider=custom:opencode-zen model=deepseek-v4-flash-free`.

4. `update_session_model()` fires and writes `model='deepseek-v4-flash-free'` to the `sessions` table. Inspect `model_config` JSON — it contains `{"max_iterations": 150, "reasoning_config": {...}, "gateway_runtime": {"provider": "custom:opencode-zen", ...}}` but **no top-level `model` or `provider` key**.

5. Resume the session (`hermes --continue` or `hermes --resume <id>`, or just reopen in Desktop).

6. **Every turn fails**: `provider=nvidia base_url=https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1 model=deepseek-v4-flash-free` → `openai.NotFoundError: 404 page not found`, retried 3×, then aborts.

## Expected Behavior

On session resume, the runtime should restore the **same provider+model pair that was active when the session was last used**. Either:
- `update_session_model()` should also persist the `provider` (and `model` for consistency) into the `model_config` JSON blob, **or**
- The session-resume code in `api_server.py:~2700` / `gateway/run.py::_resolve_session_agent_runtime` should fall back to `gateway_runtime.provider` when the `model_config` blob lacks a top-level `provider` key.

## Actual Behavior

```
2026-08-05 11:25:34,637 INFO run_agent: OpenAI client closed (stream_error_cleanup, shared=False, tcp_force_closed=1)
    provider=nvidia base_url=https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1 model=deepseek-v4-flash-free
2026-08-05 11:25:34,638 WARNING agent.conversation_loop: API call failed (attempt 2/3) error_type=NotFoundError
    provider=nvidia base_url=https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1 model=deepseek-v4-flash-free
    summary=HTTP 404: 404 page not found
2026-08-05 11:25:40,055 ERROR agent.chat_completion_helpers: Streaming failed before delivery: 404 page not found
openai.NotFoundError: 404 page not found
```

The runtime reads:
- `model` from the `sessions.model` column → `"deepseek-v4-flash-free"` ✓ (correct, set by `update_session_model`)
- `provider` from `config.yaml` `model.provider` → `"nvidia"` ✗ (WRONG — should be `custom:opencode-zen`, the provider that actually serves `deepseek-v4-flash-free`)

NVIDIA NIM doesn't serve `deepseek-v4-flash-free` → unconditional 404.

## Root Cause

**`hermes_state.py:update_session_model()` (~line 4315)** updates only the `model` column and **strips** `browser_model_lock` from `model_config` — it never writes `model` or `provider` into the blob:

```python
conn.execute(
    """UPDATE sessions SET
       model = ?,
       model_config = CASE
           WHEN model_config IS NULL THEN NULL
           WHEN json_valid(model_config)
               THEN json_remove(model_config, '$.browser_model_lock')
           ELSE model_config
       END,
       system_prompt = NULL,
       system_prompt_hash = NULL
       WHERE id = ?""",
    (model, session_id),
)
```

Meanwhile the session-resume path in **`api_server.py:_create_agent() (~line 2700)`** uses `config.yaml`'s `model.provider` as the authority when the `model_config` blob has no top-level `provider`:

```python
elif session_row_model and not confirmed_runtime_lock:
    current_provider = _clean_request_string(runtime_kwargs.get("provider"))
    # ↑ this is "nvidia" from config.yaml, NOT the session's actual provider
    provider_runtime = _resolve_provider_runtime(current_provider, ...)
    model = resolve_effective_model(None, session_row_model, model)
    # ↑ model = "deepseek-v4-flash-free" from session column
    # → POST deepseek-v4-flash-free to nvidia → 404
```

The `gateway_runtime.provider` key inside `model_config` **does** hold the correct provider (`"custom:opencode-zen"`), but the resume code does **not** read it as a fallback source for the provider.

## Impact

- Every session that was last used on a **cross-provider fallback** is broken on resume.
- The user sees 3× retries → 3× `404 page not found` → dead session.
- Affects both CLI (`hermes --resume` / `hermes --continue`) and gateway (Desktop, Telegram, Discord, etc.).
- In the affected installation, **128 sessions** were found with this mismatch.

## Workaround

Manual DB repair — add `model` and `provider` keys to the `model_config` blob:

```python
import sqlite3, json
con = sqlite3.connect("~/.hermes/state.db")
cur = con.cursor()
cur.execute("SELECT id, model, model_config FROM sessions WHERE model = 'deepseek-v4-flash-free'")
for sid, model, mc_raw in cur.fetchall():
    mc = json.loads(mc_raw) if mc_raw else {}
    if "provider" not in mc:
        mc["model"] = model
        mc["provider"] = "custom:opencode-zen"  # the provider that actually serves this model
        cur.execute("UPDATE sessions SET model_config = ? WHERE id = ?", (json.dumps(mc), sid))
con.commit()
```

## Suggested Fix

**Option A (minimal):** In `update_session_model()`, also merge `{"model": <model>, "provider": <provider>}` into the `model_config` JSON blob (needs the provider to be passed as a parameter — the gateway's `/model` handler already knows it).

**Option B (defensive):** In the session-resume path, when `model_config` has no top-level `provider` but **does** have `gateway_runtime.provider`, fall back to that instead of `config.yaml`'s `model.provider`.

Both could be applied — A fixes the write side, B makes the read side resilient to legacy sessions.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: current (config schema v32+)
- Platform: TUI / Desktop / gateway
- OS: Linux 6.12 (Debian 13)
- Primary: `nvidia` / `z-ai/glm-5.2`
- Fallback: `custom:opencode-zen` / `deepseek-v4-flash-free`

## Related

- #56885 — credential pool desync (runtime, same session; this bug is the persistence-side sibling)
- #15743 — fallback ignores its own `base_url` (runtime; also 404 on mismatched provider)
- #44070 — Desktop-specific 404 after first turn, model switch fails to recover

items.body:
> **Disclosure:** This report was drafted by an AI assistant (Claude) working through a real,
> interactive troubleshooting session on my self-hosted deployment. All stack dumps, logs and
> timelines below come from that live environment, and the proposed fix has been applied and
> validated in production there before filing.


## Bug Description

When a tool executed on the **sequential** path (`execute_tool_calls_sequential`, reached via
`_execute_tool_calls` or `execute_tool_calls_segmented`) blocks indefinitely inside its
awaitable, the conversation turn hangs **forever with zero observable symptoms**: no log line,
no error, no follow-up API call, `ended_at`/`end_reason` stay NULL, `/api/status` reports
`active_agents: 0`, and the TUI/dashboard spins on "ruminating…" indefinitely.

The concurrent path is protected by `HERMES_CONCURRENT_TOOL_TIMEOUT_S` (default 420s), but the
sequential path has **no deadline at all**. The final synchronous execution funnel,
`relay_tools._run_awaitable`, is a bare `asyncio.run(value)` with no timeout:

```python
# agent/relay_tools.py
def _run_awaitable(value: Any) -> Any:
    if not inspect.isawaitable(value):
        return value
    try:
        asyncio.get_running_loop()
    except RuntimeError:
        return asyncio.run(value)   # <-- unbounded
    raise RuntimeError(...)
```

Captured live via a `faulthandler` SIGUSR2 all-threads dump while a session was wedged — the
turn thread parked in the event loop's selector with nothing arriving:

```
Thread 0x00007f9b6dffb6c0 (most recent call first):
  File ".../selectors.py", line 452 in select
  File ".../asyncio/base_events.py", line 2004 in _run_once
  ...
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/relay_tools.py", line 120 in _run_awaitable
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/relay_tools.py", line 49 in execute
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/tool_executor.py", line 516 in _run_agent_tool_execution_middleware
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/tool_executor.py", line 1718 in execute_tool_calls_sequential
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/tool_executor.py", line 2065 in execute_tool_calls_segmented

  File "/opt/hermes/run_agent.py", line 7653 in run_conversation
  File "/opt/hermes/tui_gateway/server.py", line 9648 in run
```

In our incidents the wedged tool was a **local `skill_view`** (also observed with `read_file` /
`search_files`), so this is not limited to network tools; any awaitable that never resolves is
enough. Related: the same underlying wedge also starves the concurrent path's start-order gate —
filed separately as [Issue 2 — `_begin_in_order` unbounded wait / false timeout attribution /
thread leak], same incident, independent code path.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the gateway/dashboard (TUI session; observed with `provider: openai-codex` and
   `openrouter` alike — provider-independent).
2. Issue a prompt that triggers a multi-tool turn where a tool lands on the sequential execution
   path and its awaitable blocks (in our environment a research prompt reliably wedged a
   `skill_view`; any tool whose awaitable never resolves reproduces it).
3. Observe the turn never completes: no error, no timeout, no further API calls. The stack above
   is what a `faulthandler.dump_traceback(all_threads=True)` shows at that moment.

Deterministic reproduction without waiting for a natural wedge: monkey-patch any tool's execute
to `await asyncio.Event().wait()` and call it on the sequential path.

## Expected Behavior

A tool execution that exceeds a bounded ceiling should fail with a visible tool-error result
(like concurrent-batch timeouts do), letting the turn continue and the model/user react.

## Actual Behavior

The turn hangs forever. Nothing is written to `agent.log` after the last successful event; the
session's `ended_at`/`end_reason` remain NULL; the client shows a spinner indefinitely. Only a
process restart (or client abandon) ends it.

## Affected Component

Agent Core

## Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (reproduced on TUI/dashboard sessions; platform-independent)

## Debug Report

Full root-cause analysis with `faulthandler` all-threads dumps and exact code references is
included below; a sanitized `hermes debug` report is available on request (withheld from the
public issue as it adds no diagnostic value beyond the fields above).

## Operating System

Debian 12 host / official Docker image `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v2026.8.3` (linux/amd64)

## Python Version

3.13.5 (image venv)

## Hermes Version

v0.20.0 (2026.8.3); also reproduced on v0.19.1 (2026.7.30)

## Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

Timeline of one silent occurrence (all timestamps CEST, `agent.log`):

```
14:03:32 INFO  ... API call #4: in=44721 ... latency=9.6s
14:05:32 WARNING ... concurrent tool batch timed out after 120.0s; 4 tool(s) still running: read_file, search_files, search_files, web_extract
(no further session output, ever — no API #5, no error, no traceback; session ended_at=NULL)
```

With the proposed fix applied locally, the identical workload instead produced:

```
17:12:44 TimeoutError               <- asyncio.wait_for ceiling
17:12:44 INFO ... tool skill_view failed (420.11s): Error executing tool 'skill_view':
17:14:56 INFO ... API call #3 ...   <- turn recovered
17:16:04 INFO ... Turn ended: reason=text_response(finish_reason=stop)
```

## Root Cause Analysis (optional)

`relay_tools._run_awaitable` runs tool awaitables with a bare `asyncio.run()`; no layer of the
sequential path (`execute_tool_calls_sequential` → `_run_agent_tool_execution_middleware` →
`relay execute`) imposes any deadline. `HERMES_CONCURRENT_TOOL_TIMEOUT_S` only guards the
concurrent executor's `futures.wait` loop. The Codex/stream watchdogs guard API calls, not tool
execution. Result: one non-resolving awaitable = permanently wedged turn with no diagnostics.

## Proposed Fix (optional)

Bound the funnel (validated in production on our deployment — converted the permanent hang into
a recoverable tool error and the turn completed):

```python
    try:
        asyncio.get_running_loop()
    except RuntimeError:
        try:
            _ceiling = float(os.getenv("HERMES_TOOL_EXECUTION_CEILING_S", "420"))
        except ValueError:
            _ceiling = 420.0
        if _ceiling > 0:
            return asyncio.run(asyncio.wait_for(value, timeout=_ceiling))
        return asyncio.run(value)
```

420s default sits above every stock per-tool budget (`web_extract` 360s, typical terminal
timeouts); `0` opts out. On expiry, `TimeoutError` propagates through the existing error
handling and surfaces as a normal failed-tool result. An equivalent deadline directly in
`execute_tool_calls_sequential` would also work if a per-callsite budget is preferred.

## Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

Yes — a PR implementing this fix (with tests, validated in production) accompanies this issue.

---

items.body:
> **Disclosure:** This report was drafted by an AI assistant (Claude) working through a real,
> interactive troubleshooting session on my self-hosted deployment. All stack dumps, logs and
> timelines below come from that live environment, and the proposed fix has been applied and
> validated in production there before filing.


## Bug Description

`execute_tool_calls_concurrent`'s start-ordering gate parks every worker on a timeout-less
`Condition.wait_for` until all earlier-ordered tools have advanced:

```python
# agent/tool_executor.py (~line 746)
def _begin_in_order(order: int, callback=None) -> None:
    nonlocal next_start_order
    with start_condition:
        start_condition.wait_for(lambda: order == next_start_order)   # <-- no timeout
        try:
            if callback is not None:
                callback()
        finally:
            next_start_order += 1
            start_condition.notify_all()
```

If the gate-holding tool blocks during its dispatch/authorization (observed live: a `skill_view`
whose awaitable never resolved; historically also the smart-approval auxiliary LLM call when the
provider silently drops the request), three things go wrong at once:

1. **Every later-ordered tool in the batch is starved** — it never starts.
2. When `HERMES_CONCURRENT_TOOL_TIMEOUT_S` fires, those never-started tools are **reported as
   "timed out"** (`Error executing tool 'X': timed out after 120.0s`) — misleading, since
   sub-second local tools (`read_file`, `search_files`) get blamed while having done zero work.
   The model then reasons/retries against false failure information.
3. The batch is abandoned (`executor.shutdown(wait=False)`), but the parked workers **leak
   permanently** — `f.cancel()` cannot cancel running threads, the per-thread interrupt flag is
   never checked inside `wait_for`, and the condition is never notified again.

Captured live (SIGUSR2 `faulthandler` all-threads dump, ~60s **after** the batch deadline had
"cleaned up" the batch — these workers are already leaked at this point):

```
Thread 0x00007f659c2fa6c0 (most recent call first):
  File ".../threading.py", line 359 in wait
  File ".../threading.py", line 394 in wait_for
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/tool_executor.py", line 750 in _begin_in_order
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/tool_executor.py", line 809 in _advance_start
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/tool_executor.py", line 409 in _advance_start_order
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/tool_executor.py", line 481 in _authorized_dispatch
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/tool_executor.py", line 505 in <lambda>
  File "/opt/hermes/hermes_cli/middleware.py", line 215 in run_tool_execution_middleware
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/tool_executor.py", line 502 in _hermes_pipeline
  File "/opt/hermes/agent/relay_tools.py", line 40 in invoke
(second identical thread omitted)
```

Related: the wedged gate-holder itself is unbounded on the sequential path too — filed
separately as [Issue 1 — sequential tool execution has no deadline], same incident, independent
code path.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Trigger a turn that batches several parallel-safe tools (e.g. `read_file` + `search_files` +
   `web_search` + `skill_view`).
2. Have the earliest-ordered tool block during dispatch (naturally occurring in our environment;
   deterministically: monkey-patch one tool's dispatch to sleep forever).
3. Observe: none of the later tools ever start; at the batch deadline they are all reported
   "timed out after 120.0s" despite normally completing in ≤0.5s on the same inputs; a
   subsequent all-threads dump still shows workers parked at `_begin_in_order`.

## Expected Behavior

A wedged earlier tool should not indefinitely park later workers; batch-deadline attribution
should distinguish "never started (gate-starved)" from "started and overran"; abandoned workers
should not leak parked forever.

## Actual Behavior

All three of the above. Repeated across four separate sessions in one day; leaked parked threads
confirmed by dump after batch abandonment.

## Affected Component

Agent Core

## Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (TUI/dashboard sessions; platform-independent)

## Debug Report

Full root-cause analysis with `faulthandler` all-threads dumps and exact code references is
included below; a sanitized `hermes debug` report is available on request (withheld from the
public issue as it adds no diagnostic value beyond the fields above).

## Operating System

Debian 12 host / official Docker image `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v2026.8.3` (linux/amd64)

## Python Version

3.13.5 (image venv)

## Hermes Version

v0.20.0 (2026.8.3); also reproduced on v0.19.1 (2026.7.30)

## Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

Characteristic signature (repeated in 4 sessions, timestamps CEST):

```
17:05:43 INFO  ... API call #1 ... latency=9.8s
17:07:44 WARNING ... concurrent tool batch timed out after 120.0s; 7 tool(s) still running: skill_view, skill_view, skill_view, web_search, web_search
```

With a bounded gate applied locally (proposed fix below), the same workload instead logged:

```
17:07:44 WARNING ... start-order gate timed out (order=3 next=0); proceeding out of order
17:07:47 INFO ... tool web_search completed (123.24s, 19983 chars)     <- 3s of real work once released
17:09:47 INFO ... tool skill_view completed (243.39s, 6532 chars)
17:09:48 INFO ... tool search_files completed (244.01s, 1246 chars)
...
17:16:04 INFO ... Turn ended: reason=text_response(finish_reason=stop)  <- turn completed
```

## Root Cause Analysis (optional)

The gate serializes tool *starts* (so authorization/approval prompts fire in submission order),
but assumes the holder always advances. Any blocking dispatch violates that assumption, and
nothing bounds the wait: the deadline loop only watches futures, `f.cancel()` is a no-op on
running threads, the interrupt flag isn't polled inside `wait_for`, and after abandonment nobody
ever notifies the condition again — so the parked workers are permanent. The batch-timeout
message then attributes the failure to the starved tools rather than the holder.

## Proposed Fix (optional)

Bound the wait; on expiry, proceed out of order (worst case: interleaved approval prompts —
strictly better than permanent starvation). Validated in production on our deployment:

```python
def _begin_in_order(order: int, callback=None) -> None:
    nonlocal next_start_order
    with start_condition:
        # Wake when the counter reaches OR passes us, so one worker's
        # timeout-jump releases every skipped worker immediately.
        in_order = start_condition.wait_for(
            lambda: next_start_order >= order, timeout=120.0
        )
        if not in_order:
            logger.warning(
                "start-order gate timed out (order=%d next=%d); proceeding out of order",
                order, next_start_order,
            )
        try:
            if callback is not None:
                callback()
        finally:
            next_start_order = max(next_start_order, order + 1)
            start_condition.notify_all()
```

Two notes from validating an earlier variant that kept the exact-match predicate
(`order == next_start_order`): it works, but a timeout-jump strands the skipped workers, which
then each burn their own full timeout (observed as staggered releases at 120s/240s/360s). The
`>=` predicate above releases them all at once. Additionally, distinguishing "gate-starved,
never started" from "started and overran" in the batch-timeout attribution would remove the
misleading `timed out` blame on sub-second tools.

## Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

Yes — a PR implementing this fix (validated in production) accompanies this issue.

---

*Pre-submission notes: searched existing issues (nearest: #21444, #29418 — provider-side silent drops; #40342, #41038 — TUI indicator symptoms; none cover this defect). Reproduced on latest v2026.8.3 (v0.20.0) and on v2026.7.30 (v0.19.1).*

items.body:
# Bug: Gateway crashes with exit(1) during preflight compaction on restart

## Summary
When the Hermes gateway restarts and has a session whose history exceeds the preflight compression threshold (98,304 tokens), the **preflight compression step crashes the process with exit(1)** instead of completing compaction. The gateway then flip-flops between `failed` and `active` on every restart, or fails entirely and requires HA failover.

## Environment
- Hermes Agent v0.19.0 (2026.7.20), commit `4c9628ea` (local), upstream `b3e45a3d`
- Linux (DigitalOcean droplet, 1GB RAM), Python 3.11.15, systemd (`Restart=always`)
- Provider: Alibaba ModelStudio (`qwen3.8-max`) / Nous billing
- State DB: SQLite, WAL mode, ~347MB

## Repro sequence (observed 5 times over 5 days)
Every gateway restart with a large session present produces:

```
Stopping hermes-gateway.service
gateway.run: Shutdown context: signal=SIGTERM
📦 Preflight compression: ~119,530 tokens >= 98,304 threshold. This may take a moment.
🗜️ Compacting context — summarizing earlier conversation...
systemd[1]: hermes-gateway.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
```

The process exits with code 1 **during** the compaction step, never reaching a healthy running state.

## Root-cause evidence (from state.db `sessions` table)
The oversized session (`20260710_141554_44ed3b`, desktop-origin) carried:
- `message_count`: 1053, content ~6.8MB
- `input_tokens`: 8,916,484
- **`compression_failure_error`: "Request timed out."**
- **`compression_failure_cooldown_until`: set** (already hit a compression timeout previously)

The `Request timed out` from the auxiliary/compaction model call is not being handled as a recoverable failure. Instead of skipping compaction or retrying, it propagates and kills the gateway process with a non-zero exit.

## Impact
- Gateway instability: repeated `FAILURE` + restart cycles
- HA failover triggered on primary crash (standby promoted)
- `state.db` grows unbounded (347MB) because oversized sessions are never successfully compacted
- Silent delivery gaps during the flip-flop window

## Expected behavior
- A compaction timeout/failure should be caught, logged, and **not** crash the gateway. The gateway should start; the oversized session remains un-compacted (or compaction is deferred / retried with a longer timeout).
- Preflight compaction failure should not be a fatal error in the startup path.

## Suggested fix direction
1. Wrap the preflight compaction call so a model/provider timeout raises a recoverable exception (or is caught) instead of propagating to `sys.exit(1)`.
2. Respect `compression_failure_cooldown_until` — if a session already hit a compression failure, skip preflight compaction for it on startup rather than retrying and crashing.
3. Consider a cap on preflight-compaction attempts per session per restart.

## Regression reference
- `tests/run_agent/test_413_compression.py` covers preflight compression happy path but apparently not the provider-timeout-during-compaction crash path.
- Known related: `tests/agent/test_auxiliary_client.py` references "Preflight compression's exact failure (#23670): provider auto →".

## Workaround applied in production
Archived and removed the oversized session from `state.db` (`DELETE FROM messages/sessions`, then `VACUUM`). After removal, two consecutive restarts complete without any `Preflight compression`/`Compacting context` output and the gateway stays `active`. This confirms the crash is tied to the oversized-session compaction path, not a general startup issue.

items.body:
# `hermes update` re-detaches HEAD after a successful pull, silently discarding the update

## Summary

`hermes update` restores the pre-update `HEAD` when it finishes. If the starting `HEAD` was a raw SHA rather than a branch, it checks that SHA back out — **throwing away the pull it just completed** and re-detaching the repo.

This is self-perpetuating. Once an install is detached, every subsequent update:

1. checks out `main`
2. pulls successfully
3. resets to `origin/main`
4. checks the original SHA back out, undoing all of it
5. prints `✓ Code updated!`
6. reinstalls Python deps and rebuilds the entire Electron app against the **stale** working tree

The user sees a long, healthy, entirely successful build log and is left on the old code. There is no error, no warning, and `hermes doctor` reports a fully healthy install.

My install ran this loop from at least 2026-07-26 until 2026-08-05 and accumulated 10,227 unapplied commits. The desktop "Update now" button inherits the same failure and presents as "app quits and never comes back," which is what I originally set out to debug.

## Evidence — `git reflog`

This is the same install throughout. No manual git operations were performed until `13:42:35` on 2026-08-05, when I diagnosed and fixed it by hand.

```
$ git -C ~/.hermes/hermes-agent reflog --date=iso

acce1a245 HEAD@{2026-07-26 21:13:42}: checkout: moving from acce1a245 to main
2be2464d2 HEAD@{2026-07-26 21:13:44}: pull --ff-only origin main: Fast-forward
2be2464d2 HEAD@{2026-07-26 21:14:11}: checkout: moving from main to main
2be2464d2 HEAD@{2026-07-26 21:14:11}: reset: moving to origin/main
acce1a245 HEAD@{2026-07-26 21:14:11}: checkout: moving from main to acce1a245   ← re-detaches

2be2464d2 HEAD@{2026-08-05 13:31:34}: checkout: moving from acce1a245 to main
fb402106f HEAD@{2026-08-05 13:31:37}: pull --ff-only origin main: Fast-forward
fb402106f HEAD@{2026-08-05 13:33:17}: checkout: moving from main to main
fb402106f HEAD@{2026-08-05 13:33:17}: reset: moving to origin/main
acce1a245 HEAD@{2026-08-05 13:33:18}: checkout: moving from main to acce1a245   ← re-detaches

fb402106f HEAD@{2026-08-05 13:42:35}: checkout: moving from acce1a245 to main   ← manual fix
241605d1e HEAD@{2026-08-05 13:56:58}: merge origin/main: Fast-forward           ← GUI update, works
```

The three operations in the final group of each run occur **within the same second** — this is the updater, not user activity. The pattern is identical across two runs ten days apart.

Note the last two lines: once `HEAD` was manually reattached to `main`, the desktop app's "Update now" button worked perfectly on the very next update. The button was never broken.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent 0.15.1 (2026.5.29) → 0.20.0 (2026.8.3)
- macOS Tahoe 26.5.2, Apple Silicon (M2 Max)
- Install method: `git` — stock desktop-managed install at `~/.hermes/hermes-agent`
- Python 3.11.15, Node v24.16.0

## Reproduction

```bash
cd ~/.hermes/hermes-agent
git checkout HEAD~50        # detach
hermes update               # reports success; HEAD is unchanged afterward
git branch -vv              # main advanced, HEAD still detached at HEAD~50
hermes version              # still old version, still "N commits behind"
```

**Expected:** the update applies, or fails loudly.

**Actual:** `✓ Code updated!`, full dependency install, full Electron rebuild — against source that never moved.

## Root cause (suspected)

The update flow appears to capture the starting `HEAD` and restore it on completion. That is correct when the starting point is a branch name, and destructive when it is a detached SHA: restoring re-pins the repo to the pre-update commit.

Two things turn a recoverable state into a silent, permanent one:

1. **`✓ Code updated!` is gated on the pull succeeding, not on `HEAD` having moved.** The pull genuinely does succeed — it's the restore afterward that reverts it.
2. **The dependency install and desktop rebuild run unconditionally**, producing a convincing success log built from stale source.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Don't restore a detached `HEAD` after a successful pull.** If the update reattached to the target branch to do its work, leave it there.
2. **Detect detached `HEAD` at the start** and either reattach (reusing the existing auto-stash path for the different-branch case) or fail loudly:
   ```
   ✗ Install is on a detached HEAD (acce1a245); updates cannot be applied.
     Run: git -C ~/.hermes/hermes-agent checkout main && hermes update
   ```
3. **Gate the success message on `HEAD` actually moving** — compare the pre- and post-update SHA of `HEAD`, not of the remote ref. This alone would have surfaced the problem on day one.
4. **Add a `hermes doctor` check** for a detached install. Doctor reported a clean bill of health for the entire duration.

## Related surface: the desktop app

The GUI "Update now" button inherits this and presents it as a hang — the app quits to update, the update self-reverts, and nothing relaunches. Users will file this as a desktop bug. The About pane's `Branch main · Commit <sha>` line is a good signal, but there's no equivalent from the CLI and no indication when the branch is absent.

## Workaround

```bash
cd ~/.hermes/hermes-agent
git checkout main
hermes update
hermes desktop --force-build   # packaged Electron app was built from the stale source
```

Users should also check `git branch --show-current` before updating — if it prints nothing, the update will silently no-op.

items.body:
## Bug Description

On native Windows, `hermes update` can appear stuck for 11 minutes at:

```text
→ Refreshing cua-driver (Computer Use)...
```

It eventually reports:

```text
⚠ cua-driver refreshing timed out after 660s.
```

The upstream `install.ps1` is interactive when it encounters a stale High-IL cua-driver daemon, but Hermes captures the installer's stdout while leaving stdin attached. The prompt is therefore invisible and Hermes waits for input until its watchdog expires.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Install cua-driver with the `cua-driver-serve` Scheduled Task at `RunLevel=Highest`.
2. Leave a `cua-driver` process alive while `\\.\pipe\cua-driver` is not accepting connections.
3. From a normal, non-elevated PowerShell, run `hermes update`.
4. Observe that Hermes remains at `Refreshing cua-driver` for 660 seconds.
5. Run the installer command printed by Hermes manually. The interaction that Hermes hid is then visible:

```text
Detected STALE cua-driver daemon (...)
Process is alive but \\.\pipe\cua-driver is not accepting connections.
Fixing this requires admin to terminate the High-IL daemon process.

Trigger UAC prompt to kill the stale daemon now? [Y/n]:
```

## Expected Behavior

`hermes update` must not wait invisibly for an interactive installer prompt. When elevation is needed, Hermes should display the reason and allow the normal Windows UAC prompt to appear. Users should not have to launch the original shell as Administrator.

## Actual Behavior

Hermes prints only `Refreshing cua-driver`, waits silently for 660 seconds, kills the installer process tree, and instructs the user to rerun the upstream installer manually.

Relevant `~\AppData\Local\hermes\logs\update.log` excerpt:

```text
→ Refreshing cua-driver (Computer Use)...
⚠ cua-driver refreshing timed out after 660s.
  Re-run manually: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/trycua/cua/main/libs/cua-driver/scripts/install.ps1 | iex"
```

This has occurred repeatedly, including on 2026-08-05 with current `main`.

## Affected Component

- Setup / Installation
- Tools (Computer Use)

## Messaging Platform

N/A (CLI only)

## Debug Report

Generated locally with `hermes debug share --local`; no paste-service upload was made because the minimal evidence is included here.

```text
version:     0.20.0 [fb402106] (2026-08-05)
upstream:    d1f9e777
os:          Windows 10 AMD64 (Windows 11 host)
python:      3.11.15 (Hermes managed runtime)
install:     native Windows, git
cua-driver:  0.17.0
```

## Operating System

Windows 11, native Windows installation

## Python Version

Hermes managed runtime: Python 3.11.15. Host `python --version`: Python 3.10.10.

## Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.20.0 (2026.8.3), upstream `d1f9e777`, local/current checkout `fb402106`.

## Root Cause Analysis

`hermes_cli/update_cmd.py` calls:

```python
install_cua_driver(
    upgrade=True,
    require_confirmed_update=True,
    show_installer_progress=False,
)
```

`install_cua_driver()` then calls `_run_cua_driver_installer(verbose=False)`. On that path, `hermes_cli/tools_config.py` starts PowerShell with `stdout=subprocess.PIPE` and `stderr=subprocess.STDOUT`, while stdin is inherited.

The current upstream CUA installer calls `Repair-CuaDriverStaleDaemon`, whose default path uses:

```powershell
$ans = Read-Host "Trigger UAC prompt to kill the stale daemon now? [Y/n]"
```

Because stdout is captured, the user cannot see the question. Because stdin remains attached, `Read-Host` waits rather than failing fast. Hermes only regains control when `_CUA_INSTALLER_TIMEOUT` expires after 660 seconds.

The upstream helper has an internal `-AutoConfirm` switch, but `install.ps1` currently exposes no parameter or documented environment option that a caller such as Hermes can set.

Related but non-duplicate issues:

- #71319 fixed Windows orphaned installer processes and stale lock recovery, not hidden interactive prompts.
- trycua/cua#2137 and trycua/cua#2809 cover stale daemon/autostart upgrade paths, not Hermes' captured prompt.

## Proposed Fix

Immediate Hermes-side fix:

- On Windows, do not hide output from an upstream installer that may require interaction, or forward installer output incrementally while preserving stdin.
- Keep the process-tree timeout cleanup introduced for #71319.
- Add a regression test with an installer child that writes a prompt and waits for input; verify the prompt is visible instead of silently waiting.

Preferred coordinated fix:

1. Upstream exposes an installer-level option such as `-AutoConfirmStaleDaemonRepair` (or a documented equivalent).
2. Hermes invokes the downloaded script with that option for an interactive `hermes update`.
3. Windows still displays the actual UAC consent dialog; only the redundant text Y/n question is pre-confirmed. Hermes should not bypass UAC or silently elevate.

## Additional Upstream Observation

During the manual retry, accepting UAC did not complete recovery:

```text
Elevated kill did not complete (UAC cancelled or pipe still dead).
```

The reported process PID changed after elevation, suggesting that the old daemon may have been killed/restarted but the replacement pipe never became healthy. That may warrant a separate `trycua/cua` report if it remains reproducible after a release containing trycua/cua#2809.

## Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

Yes. I am willing to help validate or submit a focused fix after maintainers confirm the preferred Hermes/upstream interface.

items.title: Wedged authorization gate hangs the turn and defeats the concurrent batch deadline entirely

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Summary

A tool wedged inside the concurrent **authorization** gate hangs the whole turn indefinitely — and unlike the start-order gate wedge fixed in #79705, this one defeats the batch deadline entirely, so nothing ever times the batch out.

Two coupled problems in `_ConcurrentToolAuthorizationGate` (`agent/tool_executor.py:345-387`):

1. `self._serialization_lock` (:349, acquired at :362) is an **unbounded** blocking acquire. If the worker holding it wedges — a `pre_tool_block` plugin that hangs, or an approval round-trip to a client that went away — every other worker needing authorization blocks behind it forever.
2. While that window is open, `excluded_seconds()` (:375-382) grows **1:1 with wall clock**, and the batch-deadline loop adds it to the deadline on every poll (:1070 and :1092). So `remaining` is *constant* and the deadline never fires.

Problem 2 is the serious half. #79705 bounded the start-order gate, but this sits **upstream** of it: a worker wedged in authorization never reaches `_begin_in_order` at all, so `next_start_order` never advances — and now there is no deadline to end the turn either.

## Reproduction

Drives the real `_ConcurrentToolAuthorizationGate` from current `main` with the same arithmetic as the deadline loop, one worker wedged inside `gate.run()`:

```
sim wall clock |  excluded_seconds() |  remaining | deadline fires?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
              1s |                1.3s |     420.3s | False
             60s |               60.3s |     420.3s | False
            600s |              600.3s |     420.3s | False
          86400s |            86400.3s |     420.3s | False
```

`remaining` never decreases. `while True` at :1094 never satisfies `remaining <= 0`, and the check at :1092 never trips. At 24h simulated wall clock the batch is still "not timed out".

Algebraically: `remaining = (deadline + (now - window_started)) - now = deadline - window_started` — `now` cancels out.

## Why this is worse than the bug #79705 fixed

| | start-order gate wedge (fixed in #79705) | authorization gate wedge (this issue) |
|---|---|---|
| later workers starved | yes | yes |
| batch deadline | fires (mislabeling the parked tools) | **never fires** |
| turn outcome | ends, with wrong tool results | **hangs forever** |

The pre-#79705 behavior at least terminated via a mislabeled timeout. This path just wedges the session.

## Suggested fix

**Bound the acquire** using the idiom already in the tree (`tools/daemon_pool.py:43`, `agent/conversation_compression.py:526`):

```python
acquired = self._serialization_lock.acquire(timeout=_AUTHORIZATION_GATE_TIMEOUT_S)
try:
    if not acquired:
        logger.warning("authorization gate timed out; running prompt unserialized")
    return callback()
finally:
    if acquired:
        self._serialization_lock.release()
```

Losing serialization degrades to interleaved approval prompts — the same tradeoff #79705 accepted for the start-order gate, and strictly better than a hung turn.

**Cap the exclusion separately.** Bounding the lock alone does not fix problem 2: the wedge can be *inside* `callback()`, which holds the window open regardless. `excluded_seconds()` needs a ceiling so an open window cannot indefinitely defeat the deadline.

Design question worth settling: a legitimate approval round-trip genuinely can exceed any fixed bound (a user answering a prompt 10 minutes later), and excluding that time from the deadline is *deliberate* — that's what the mechanism is for. So the cap probably wants to distinguish "waiting on a human" from "wedged in a plugin" rather than being a flat number. Flagging rather than assuming.

## Notes

- Pre-existing on `main`; not introduced by #79705. Found while reviewing that PR and deliberately scoped out of it, since bounding this touches approval serialization.
- `_ConcurrentToolAuthorizationGate` has no test coverage today: no test references `_ConcurrentToolAuthorizationGate`, `excluded_seconds`, or `_serialization_lock`.
- Repro imports the real class, no mocks, verified against `upstream/main`.

items.body:
Since 2026-08-05 ~21:56 UTC every gateway turn on the Anthropic OAuth path fails:

```text
HTTP 400 invalid_request_error: Third-party apps now draw from your extra usage,
not your plan limits. Add more at claude.ai/settings/usage and keep going.
```

Small `-z` one-shots keep working, which makes this look intermittent. It is not.

## What I measured

I captured a failing request from `request_dump_*.json` and replayed it against
`api.anthropic.com/v1/messages`, stripping one suspect field per variant.

| Variant | Result |
|---|---|
| full replay | 400 |
| without tools (37 removed) | 400 |
| `max_tokens` 128000 → 8192 | 400 |
| system = Claude Code prefix only (block 0) | **200** |
| Claude Code prefix + block 1 (8,736 ch — the Hermes identity prompt) | **400** |
| Claude Code prefix + block 2 (33,913 ch workspace context) | **200** |
| minimal message, same prefix | **200** |

Block 1 flips the verdict in both directions. Size is not the trigger — block 2
is ~4× larger and passes. Tools and `max_tokens` are not the trigger either.

Then I wired a `claude setup-token` credential (`sk-ant-oat01-…`) alongside the
PKCE one and replayed the same unmodified body through both:

| Credential | Result |
|---|---|
| `hermes_pkce` | 400 |
| Claude Code subscription setup token | 400 |

Same body, same minute, both rejected. The classification is made from
**system-prompt content**, independent of which credential presents it.

## Why block 1 specifically

`agent/anthropic_adapter.py:2888-2907` prepends the Claude Code identity prefix on
every OAuth request, then rewrites product names in the whole system prompt:

```python
text = text.replace("Hermes Agent", "Claude Code")
text = text.replace("Hermes agent", "Claude Code")
text = text.replace("hermes-agent", "claude-code")
text = text.replace("Nous Research", "Anthropic")
```

The comment says this is "to avoid Anthropic's server-side content filters". The
rewrite is also partial — bare "Hermes" survives (e.g. "When the user needs help
with Hermes itself…"), so the resulting prompt is neither Hermes' nor Claude
Code's. Anthropic now appears to classify exactly this shape as a third-party
client, and the new policy routes third-party traffic to extra-usage billing;
accounts without an extra-usage balance get a hard 400 instead of drawing on the
plan.

## Ask

Is the rename/prefix behaviour still intended now that Anthropic classifies on
prompt content? Options I can see, roughly in order of honesty:

1. Drop the identity prefix and the product-name rewrites for OAuth requests and
   let Hermes identify as Hermes, accepting third-party billing.
2. Make it opt-in behind a config key so operators choose, and document that the
   default now yields a 400 on subscription accounts with no extra-usage balance.
3. At minimum, surface a clearer error — the current message sends users to
   claude.ai/settings/usage when the actionable cause is on the Hermes side.

Happy to test a patch against my deployment; the replay harness is ~120 lines and
I can share it.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.20.0 (2026.8.3), Docker, `nousresearch/hermes-agent:latest`
- model `claude-opus-5`, provider `anthropic`, OAuth (`hermes_pkce`)
- reproduced on 2026-08-05/06 across many turns; 599 calls on the same config
  succeeded in the hour before the flip, so nothing changed locally

items.title: Cron inactivity watchdog blind spot: unbounded pre-run blocking (_terminal_cwd_lock, in-process jobs RLock) leaves jobs wedged in 'running' with no logs

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

labels.name: sweeper:risk-automation
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may affect CI, automerge, label sync, or maintainer automation

items.body:
## Bug Description

Cron's inactivity watchdog only covers `agent.run_conversation()`. A job's execution row is marked `running` much earlier, and several pre-watchdog phases can block **unbounded** — leaving jobs wedged in `running` with zero log output until gateway restart. This is the best-fit explanation for #79244 (3 concurrent jobs stuck 12–17 min, no 600s timeout log, cleared only by restart).

## Unbounded pre-watchdog blocking points

1. **`_terminal_cwd_lock` (readers-writer lock)** — `cron/scheduler.py` ~3117-3121:
   - Workdir jobs `acquire_write()` and hold it for their **entire agent run**.
   - Workdir-less jobs `acquire_read()` — which blocks not only while a writer is active but **whenever a writer is merely waiting** (writer-preference, see `_ReadWriteLock.acquire_read`).
   - Neither acquire has a timeout. One wedged or long-running workdir job ⇒ every concurrently firing job parks in `running` before its watchdog loop even starts, silently.

2. **In-process `_jobs_file_lock` RLock** (`cron/jobs.py` ~299) is unbounded. The cross-process flock is bounded at 30s (#60703), but a thread wedged *inside* the critical section freezes every other job's `_heartbeat_run_claim_if_due()` → and that call happens **before** the idle check on each 5s watchdog iteration, so the watchdog loop itself can stall mid-iteration.

3. Everything else between the `running` mark (~scheduler.py:3973) and the watchdog attach (~:3607) — MCP init is try/except-bounded, SessionDB init is 10s-bounded, but the phase as a whole has no umbrella deadline.

## Expected behavior

Either:
- the inactivity watchdog's coverage starts when the execution is marked `running` (umbrella deadline on the pre-run phase), or
- the pre-run blocking points get explicit timeouts (`acquire_read/acquire_write(timeout=...)` with a clear error), or
- at minimum, a periodic "job X waiting on cwd-lock for Ns" log so operators can see where a stuck job is parked instead of a silent `running` row.

## Impact

Matches the #79244 incident shape: multiple jobs firing within minutes of each other, all stuck in `running` for 12+ minutes, no timeout error, manual gateway restart required. The watchdog reorder proposed in PR #79313 (closed) would not have helped, since the watchdog never fired in this window.

## References

- #79244 — the incident report (evidence: durations 772–1032s, no 600s TimeoutError)
- #60703 — bounded the cross-process flock at 30s (the in-process RLock remains unbounded)
- #79173 — bounded the hung-non-streaming-call class; does not cover lock wedges

items.title: weixin/email pollers leak proxied TCP sockets on macOS → fd exhaustion → gateway crash (Errno 24)

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
## Summary

On macOS, a launchd-managed Hermes gateway (v0.20.0) leaks TCP file descriptors when the **weixin** and **email/IMAP** platform pollers route through a local HTTP proxy (Clash on `127.0.0.1:7890`). Sockets opened per poll cycle are never reclaimed, so the fd count grows monotonically until it hits the macOS default soft limit of **256**, at which point the gateway can no longer open `state.db`, `.drain_request.json`, or any file — cascading into `[Errno 24] Too many open files` and a crash. launchd (`KeepAlive`) respawns it, surfacing to the user as *"Sorry, I encountered an unexpected error."*

This is distinct from the fd-limit/plist issues #30230 and #36899 (which blame MCP subprocesses and the missing `NumberOfFiles` limit respectively). Here the **source of the leak is the weixin/email poller's proxied connections**, not MCP, and raising the plist limit only delays the crash rather than stopping the growth.

## Root cause (measured)

Live capture of the gateway process just before a crash:

```
fd total (numeric fds only): 256   ← pinned at the macOS soft limit
connections to proxy :7890:  216   ← 84% of all fds
```

After a `launchctl kickstart -k` restart, same process a few seconds later:

```
fd total: 16
connections to proxy :7890: 2
```

So ~214 of the 216 proxy connections were **leaked** (not in legitimate concurrent use). The count climbs steadily with each weixin/email poll cycle and never drops back down on its own.

### Aggravating factor: DNS-failure retry storm

The gateway error log shows the weixin and email pollers repeatedly failing to resolve their hosts **through the proxy**:

```
ERROR gateway.platforms.weixin: [Weixin] poll error (1/3): Cannot connect to host ilinkai.weixin.qq.com:443 ssl:default [nodename nor servname provided, or not known]
ERROR hermes_plugins.email_platform.adapter: [Email] IMAP fetch error: [Errno 8] nodename nor servname provided, or not known
```

Each failed poll appears to open a proxy socket that is then abandoned without being closed, so DNS/proxy resolution failures **accelerate** the leak. The same log is flooded with the downstream symptom:

```
WARNING gateway.drain_control: drain-control: failed to read /Users/<user>/.hermes/.drain_request.json: [Errno 24] Too many open files
WARNING tools.terminal_tool: Error in cleanup thread: [Errno 24] Too many open files
OSError: [Errno 24] Too many open files
```

## Impact

- Gateway crashes roughly once its uptime lets the leak reach 256 fds; users on Telegram/weixin see *"unexpected error"* replies.
- Restart is only a temporary fix — fd count starts climbing again immediately.
- Worst on machines where a channel's host fails to resolve through the proxy (retry storm), and on macOS specifically because of the low 256 default soft limit.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.20.0 (2026.8.3), Python 3.11.15
- macOS, user LaunchAgent `ai.hermes.gateway`
- weixin + email platforms enabled, outbound via local proxy `127.0.0.1:7890` (Clash)
- `launchctl limit maxfiles` → `256 unlimited`

## Suggested fixes

1. **Close proxied sockets on every poll cycle** — ensure the weixin and email/IMAP pollers use a pooled/`async with` client session and close connections (or reuse a single keep-alive session) instead of opening a fresh socket per poll that is never released.
2. **Release sockets on failure paths** — a failed DNS/proxy resolution must not leave a dangling connection; wrap poll attempts so the socket is closed in `finally`.
3. **Back off on repeated resolution failure** — after N consecutive `nodename nor servname` failures, exponentially back off that channel instead of hammering the proxy every interval (which both leaks fds and spams the log).
4. **fd-usage guard in the gateway loop** — log a warning when fd count exceeds ~80% of the soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE`, so the leak is visible before it becomes a crash. (Overlaps with the fd-monitoring suggestion in #30230.)

## Related

- #30230 — gateway hits the macOS 256 fd limit (attributed to MCP subprocess pipes)
- #36899 — launchd plist lacks `NumberOfFiles`, so the process inherits the low limit

Raising the plist `SoftResourceLimits.NumberOfFiles` (per #36899) mitigates the *symptom*, but this issue is specifically about the **weixin/email proxy connection leak** being the *source* of unbounded fd growth.

items.title: [Bug]: anydoc extraction stays disabled for the process lifetime after one failed first load
items.body:
### Bug Description

The anydoc-backed document extraction from #79781 caches the result of its first load attempt permanently. In `tools/read_extract.py`, `_anydoc()` sets `_anydoc_module = None` when the lazy install or the import fails, and nothing ever resets it. One bad first try (network blip during the pip install, a missing wheel for the platform, a pip race with another process, a read-only store on a managed install) disables PDF, legacy Office, OpenDocument, RTF, and EPUB extraction for the rest of the process lifetime.

This is worst exactly where extraction matters most: long-lived gateway and desktop workers. A gateway that had one transient failure at startup never converts another PDF until someone restarts it.

The first load is also unlocked. `_anydoc_module` is a process global with no synchronization, so two parallel reads of covered files on first use can both shell out to pip, or one can race the other's failure into the cache.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a fresh Hermes process in an environment where the first `firecrawl-anydoc` install attempt will fail (offline, or `pip` blocked).
2. Read a PDF with `read_file`. Extraction fails and `_anydoc_module` is cached as `None`.
3. Restore the network and install `firecrawl-anydoc` successfully.
4. Read the PDF again in the same process. Extraction is still treated as unavailable.

### Expected Behavior

A failed first load is retried after a cooldown, so a transient failure does not stick for the process lifetime. Concurrent first use performs a single install and import.

### Actual Behavior

The first failure is cached forever. Every later covered file in that process falls through to raw text or the binary guard, and parallel first use can double-install.

### Affected Component

Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

items.body:
### Bug Description

The anydoc-backed extraction from #79781 converts every covered file with no size or time budget. `_extract_anydoc` in `tools/read_extract.py` passes the path straight to `to_markdown()`, which loads the whole document through anydoc's Rust core in one shot. The read_file char budget only trims the output after conversion has already completed, so it does nothing to bound the conversion itself.

One large PDF, legacy spreadsheet, or slide deck can block a tool turn for a long time and spike RAM, on every platform, including long-lived gateway workers where a stuck turn stalls the whole session.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Install `firecrawl-anydoc` (or let the first read lazy-install it).
2. Read a very large PDF (hundreds of MB) with `read_file`.
3. The tool turn blocks inside `to_markdown` while the full document is converted, before any budget logic runs.

### Expected Behavior

Oversized documents are rejected before conversion with a clear `ExtractionError`, routing them to the existing read_file fallthrough instead of pinning the turn.

### Actual Behavior

Any size input is converted in full first, and only the resulting text is budget-checked afterwards.

### Affected Component

Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report

```shell
Not a runtime crash. Missing resource bound in tools/read_extract.py:
_extract_anydoc() calls to_markdown(path) with no size pre-check.
```

### Operating System

Windows 11

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

main @ 01a1037d1 (post-#79781)

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

`tools/read_extract.py` `_extract_anydoc()`: unlike the stdlib XLSX extractor, which at least caps rows and columns mid-parse, the anydoc path has no bound at any stage. There is also no practical timeout: the conversion is a synchronous Rust call that Python cannot cancel, so a thread-based deadline would cap the wait but leave the RAM burn running in the background. A size pre-check is the enforceable bound.

items.title: [Bug]: Email adapter swallows all fetch failures — never triggers fatal-error/reconnect path

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
### Bug Description

_fetch_new_messages() wraps its entire IMAP connect/login/select/search/fetch sequence in a single bare except Exception. On any failure it logs a generic [Email] IMAP fetch error: %s and returns the (empty) results list — identical to what it returns on a genuinely empty inbox. The caller has no way to tell "checked, nothing new" apart from "the check itself failed."

Critically, the adapter never calls its own fatal-error hook (self._fatal_error_handler, wired via set_fatal_error_handler), so the gateway's existing reconnect/backoff/status machinery — which already works correctly for startup failures via _handle_adapter_fatal_error — never learns that email is unhealthy. In practice this means extended stretches (sometimes hours) where the mailbox is unreachable, with zero reconnect attempts, zero platform-status change, and zero user-facing signal beyond a repeating log line. Only a manual gateway restart clears it.

I originally hit this on v0.15.1 and confirmed after updating to v0.20.0 that the exact same swallow-all pattern is still present — an unrelated round of hardening (malformed-response handling, sender authentication) landed in this function in between, but didn't touch the outer exception handling. So this looks like a structural gap rather than leftover stale code.


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Have the gateway running
2. Have an interruption in internet access while still on the network. 

### Expected Behavior

1. Check Imap Fails
2. Calls back to reestablish connection just like if an new connection fails.  

### Actual Behavior

Representative log excerpts across ~2 months of a persistently-running gateway:

2026-08-04 07:56:11,146 ERROR gateway.platforms.email: [Email] IMAP fetch error: The read operation timed out

2026-08-04 08:11:29,598 ERROR gateway.platforms.email: [Email] IMAP fetch error: The read operation timed out

2026-08-04 08:20:34,350 ERROR gateway.platforms.email: [Email] IMAP fetch error: The read operation timed out

No Fatal email adapter error line (the line _handle_adapter_fatal_error emits) ever appears alongside these — confirming the fatal-error path is never invoked from this function. Contrast with the startup failure path, which correctly logs Reconnecting email (attempt N)... with exponential backoff and eventually recovers on its own.

My own repro likely has an unstable network as the proximate trigger (VLAN config issue on my end causing periodic drops) — but that's exactly the kind of transient condition this code path should already tolerate gracefully via the existing reconnect system, not go silent under.


### Affected Component

Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report

```shell
Debug report uploaded:
  Report       https://paste.rs/Z5Gzl
  agent.log    https://dpaste.com/543VDD2BP
  gateway.log  https://dpaste.com/2RESM5DQA
```

### Operating System

Window 11

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.20.0 (2026.8.3) 

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

gateway/platforms/email.py
def _fetch_new_messages(self)
Looking at the full EmailAdapter class rather than just _fetch_new_messages in isolation: the adapter already has an established convention for reporting fatal errors — self._set_fatal_error(code, message, retryable=bool) — used in connect()'s missing-configuration branch. So the fix doesn't need to invent new attribute-setting; it needs to call the existing method from the place that's actually missing it.

That place is _poll_loop, not _fetch_new_messages:

async def _poll_loop(self) -> None:

    """Poll IMAP for new messages at regular intervals."""

    while self._running:

        try:

            await self._check_inbox()

        except asyncio.CancelledError:

            break

        except Exception as e:

            logger.error("[Email] Poll error: %s", e)

        await asyncio.sleep(self._poll_interval)

_check_inbox calls _fetch_new_messages, which already catches and swallows every IMAP exception internally and returns [] — so this outer except in _poll_loop rarely even fires for IMAP failures; the inner function already consumed them. And when it does fire, the loop just logs and continues forever. Nothing here ever reaches _failed_platforms or the fatal-error system, and — unlike connect(), whose failures are caught by a supervising caller one layer up that queues a retry even without an explicit _set_fatal_error call — _poll_loop is a self-contained while self._running loop with no outer supervisor at all. It is a dead end for error reporting by construction, not just by omission inside _fetch_new_messages.

Related

#18106 — same file, different symptom (iCloud response-parsing AttributeError
SSL handshake timeout). Appears to be what motivated the malformed-response guards added since v0.15.1. Confirms this function has a track record of under-handling non-happy-path IMAP responses.
#18541 — confirms the adapter is poll-based, not IDLE-based, ruling out a stale-idle-connection theory for the timeouts reported here.


### Proposed Fix (optional)

Not a rewrite — _fetch_new_messages's per-message handling and its own try/except are fine as-is. The gap is that _poll_loop has no way to escalate a sustained run of failures using the convention the adapter already has:

async def _poll_loop(self) -> None:

    """Poll IMAP for new messages at regular intervals."""

    while self._running:

        try:

            await self._check_inbox()

            self._consecutive_poll_failures = 0

        except asyncio.CancelledError:

            break

        except Exception as e:

            logger.error("[Email] Poll error: %s", e)

            self._consecutive_poll_failures = getattr(self, "_consecutive_poll_failures", 0) + 1

            if self._consecutive_poll_failures >= self._poll_failure_threshold:

                self._set_fatal_error("email_poll_failure", str(e), retryable=True)

                break  # stop polling — gateway now owns recovery via reconnect

        await asyncio.sleep(self._poll_interval)

Notes on intent, not prescribing exact numbers:

Purely additive — one counter, one call into the adapter's existing _set_fatal_error convention, one break to hand control back to the gateway's reconnect watcher instead of looping forever on a connection it no longer trusts. No change to _fetch_new_messages or per-message handling.
A threshold (_poll_failure_threshold, maybe 3–5 consecutive cycles, possibly configurable) avoids escalating on a single blip — the reconnect watcher already backs off exponentially once a platform is queued, so this just needs to get email into that queue when failure is sustained rather than momentary.
Open question I don't want to assume the answer to: does _set_fatal_error already handle any adapter-side cleanup (e.g. does it expect the caller to also flip self._running = False / call self.disconnect()), or does the caller need to do that explicitly alongside it? I inferred its signature from the one call site in connect()'s missing-config branch, but haven't seen its implementation — happy to adjust once that's confirmed.

items.title: Desktop: subagent stays 'running' forever when it times out — status vocabulary mismatch ('timeout'/'error' are not terminal in the renderer)

labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

items.body:
## Summary

When a delegated subagent times out, the desktop's subagent indicator spins indefinitely. The parent turn completes normally and the backend is fully idle, but the UI keeps showing the subagent as in-flight — so a finished answer looks unfinished, and the user waits (or interrupts) for work that already ended.

## Cause

A status vocabulary mismatch between the emitter and the store — the completion event *is* delivered, it just isn't recognized as terminal.

**Backend** — `tools/delegate_tool.py` (~2254-2266) emits the completion callback with a `timeout`/`error` status:

```python
if child_progress_cb:
    child_progress_cb(
        "subagent.complete",
        preview=(f"Timed out after {duration}s" if is_timeout else str(_timeout_exc)),
        status="timeout" if is_timeout else "error",
        duration_seconds=duration,
        summary="",
    )
```

**Renderer** — `apps/desktop/src/store/subagents.ts`:

```ts
export type SubagentStatus = 'completed' | 'failed' | 'interrupted' | 'queued' | 'running'
...
const TERMINAL: ReadonlySet<SubagentStatus> = new Set(['completed', 'failed', 'interrupted'])
```

`'timeout'` and `'error'` are in neither the type nor `TERMINAL`, so `upsertSubagent` never transitions the entry to a terminal state and the spinner persists for the life of the session.

## Repro

1. Dispatch a fan-out where at least one subagent will exceed the delegation timeout (600s default) — easiest under a slow provider window.
2. Backend logs the timeout and the parent recovers: `Subagent N timed out after 600.1s`, `✗ [3/3] <goal> (600.1s)`, parent turn ends `finish_reason=stop`.
3. Desktop still shows "1 Subagent — <goal>" with an active spinner, indefinitely. Switching sessions and back clears it (state is re-read); nothing else does.

## Observed

- Parent session's final assistant message written and turn ended cleanly; all processes idle (compute host 0.0% CPU) — confirmed backend-side.
- The orphaned subagent session is persisted with `end_reason='ws_orphan_reap'` and its full transcript (116 messages here), so its partial work is recoverable — but the UI gives no indication it ended at all.

## Suggested fix

Either normalize at the emitter (map `timeout` → `failed`, `error` → `failed`) or widen the renderer:

```ts
export type SubagentStatus =
  'completed' | 'failed' | 'interrupted' | 'queued' | 'running' | 'timeout' | 'error'

const TERMINAL: ReadonlySet<SubagentStatus> =
  new Set(['completed', 'failed', 'interrupted', 'timeout', 'error'])
```

Widening the renderer seems preferable — `timeout` and `error` are meaningfully different outcomes to surface in the UI, and collapsing them at the emitter loses that. A defensive default (treat any unrecognized status on `subagent.complete` as terminal) would also prevent the same class of drift if the backend adds statuses later.

## Environment

macOS arm64, v2026.8.3 (0.20.0) tree, locally built desktop, remote-mode backend (`hermes serve` under launchd).

items.title: vision_tools hardcodes max_tokens 2000/4000, truncating image/video analysis (contradicts auxiliary_client no-cap policy)
items.body:
**Bug**
`tools/vision_tools.py` passes hardcoded output caps on every vision call:
- image analysis: `max_tokens: 2000`
- video analysis: `max_tokens: 4000`

Long image descriptions and video analyses are silently truncated at these limits regardless of the vision model's actual capacity.

**Why this contradicts Hermes' own design**
`agent/auxiliary_client.py` (request builder, ~line 7879) states the policy explicitly: 'We do NOT cap output by default. Most chat-completions providers treat an omitted max_tokens as use the model's max output, which is what we want for auxiliary tasks (compression summaries, titles, vision, etc.) — an explicit cap only risks truncating a summary.' Vision is named in that comment, yet vision_tools is the one caller that still hardcodes a cap.

**Expected behavior**
Vision calls should omit max_tokens by default (model sizes its own response), with an optional user override.

**Fix (verified locally on 0.19.0)**
Read `auxiliary.vision.max_tokens` from config; only pass max_tokens when it is an explicit integer (treat unset or 'auto' as omit):
```python
_vmax = _vision_cfg.get("max_tokens")
...
call_kwargs = {"task": "vision", "messages": messages,
               "temperature": vision_temperature, "timeout": vision_timeout}
if _vmax is not None and str(_vmax).strip().lower() != "auto":
    call_kwargs["max_tokens"] = int(_vmax)
```
Applied at both call sites (image ~line 1242, video ~line 1753 in 0.19.0). Verified end-to-end: gemini-2.5-flash via OpenAI-compatible endpoint returned a 4,772-char analysis with finish_reason 'stop' (previously truncated at cap).

items.body:
## Summary

`hermes update` on a shallow git install triggers a **full unshallow fetch** (missing `--depth 1` in the update path) and shows **no progress output** while doing it — the terminal sits at "→ Fetching updates..." for 20+ minutes and looks hung.

## Environment

- Hermes v0.20.0 (2026.8.3), git install (installer shallow clone, `.git/shallow` present)
- Windows 10, git-bash

## Root cause 1: update path drops the depth args

`hermes_cli/update_cmd.py`:

- The `--check` path correctly detects shallow repos and appends `--depth 1` (~line 2228-2237):
  ```python
  is_shallow = (subprocess.run(git_cmd + ["rev-parse", "--is-shallow-repository"], ...).stdout.strip() == "true")
  depth_args = ["--depth", "1"] if is_shallow else []
  ```
- The **actual update path** (~line 3738) does NOT reuse `depth_args`:
  ```python
  fetch_result = subprocess.run(
      git_cmd + ["fetch", "origin", branch],   # no --depth 1
      ...
  )
  ```

Result: on a shallow install, `hermes update` unshallows the repo and drags in the entire history. Observed live: `git index-pack` receiving a pack with **179,583 objects**; ~130 KB/s on a mainland-China network, 42 MB in ~9 minutes and nowhere near done. The repo's own comment at line 2223-2227 warns this is exactly the cost the shallow clone avoided.

## Root cause 2: progress is swallowed

`capture_output=True` captures git's stderr where the progress bar lives. User sees only "→ Fetching updates..." and then nothing for tens of minutes — easy to mistake for a hang (I did; the fetch was actually making progress the whole time, verifiable via `.git/objects/pack/tmp_pack_*` growth).

## Suggested fix

Reuse `depth_args` in the update path's fetch (same as the `--check` path), and consider streaming stderr or printing a "fetching (this can take a while)..." hint when the repo is not shallow.

## Repro / evidence

- `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` → `true` on a fresh installer checkout
- `hermes update` → `git -c windows.appendAtomically=false fetch origin main` (no `--depth`) → full-history transfer
- Manual shallow fetch as a workaround completes in ~7 seconds: `git fetch --depth=1 origin main && git reset --hard origin/main`

items.body:
# [BUG] `hermes update --check` reports huge bogus "behind" count on shallow repos with pre-deepened history

**Repo:** NousResearch/hermes-agent
**File:** `hermes_cli/update_cmd.py` (lines ~2223–2237, ~2288+)
**Severity:** Medium (cosmetic but misleading; wrong update signals)

## Summary

On an install whose repo is shallow (`git clone --depth 1`, as the installer creates)
but whose history has been **deepened by prior unconstrained fetches/pulls**, the
`--depth 1` fetch in `hermes update` (and `--check`) leaves `HEAD` on a shallow
boundary commit that git cannot connect to the rest of the already-downloaded
history. `git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/<branch>` then reports a wildly inflated
"behind" number (in our case **20356 of 20357 total repo commits**), where the true
distance is ~123 commits.

## Repro (observed)

1. Install hermes-agent → repo is shallow (`git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` → `true`).
2. Over time, update via plain `git pull` / unconstrained fetch (e.g. an ops script),
   which deepens the downloaded history.
3. Run `hermes update --check` (or `hermes update --yes`):
   - `update_cmd.py` detects shallow and fetches `git fetch --depth 1 origin main`
     ("preserve the boundary and report presence-only").
   - It then counts `rev-list HEAD..origin/<branch>`.
   - Result: e.g. `behind=20356` — false; real distance was ~123 commits.
4. The apply path then does `git reset --hard origin/main`, landing `HEAD` **on** the
   new boundary commit. From then on even `git status` reports "behind by 20356
   commits" permanently (HEAD has no visible ancestors).

## Root cause

`hermes_cli/update_cmd.py` assumes a shallow repo contains *only* the tip commit
("Installer checkouts are shallow ... fetch with `--depth 1` to preserve the boundary
and report presence-only"). That assumption breaks once the same repo has been
deepened by other tooling (a plain `git fetch`/`git pull` on a shallow repo
deepens it). The `--depth 1` fetch then adds a new boundary at the tip while older
boundaries remain, and `HEAD` ends up disconnected from the downloaded history — so
`rev-list --count` counts nearly the entire repository instead of the true delta.

Evidence from the affected repo (`~/.hermes/hermes-agent`, git 2.43.0):

```
$ git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository   # before fix
true
$ git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main  # before fix (bogus)
20356
$ git rev-list --count origin/main        # total downloaded history
20357
$ git log -1 --format='%ci' HEAD          # HEAD is one day old
2026-08-05 14:00:25 +0530
$ git log origin/main --since="2026-08-05 08:00" --until="2026-08-06 06:00" --format='%h' | wc -l
93   # true distance is ~93–123 commits, NOT 20356
```

## Suggested fix

When the repo is shallow, do **not** compute a rev-list count. Options:

1. **Presence-only check:** compare SHAs (`git rev-parse HEAD` vs `git rev-parse origin/<branch>`); report "behind: yes/no" without a count.
2. If a count is desired, fetch with enough depth to make it meaningful (`--shallow-since=<date>` or `--deepen=N`), or `--unshallow` once.
3. After the apply-path `reset --hard origin/main`, run `git fetch --unshallow` if the repo previously held deeper history, so `git status` stays truthful.

## Workaround for affected users

```
cd ~/.hermes/hermes-agent
git fetch --unshallow origin    # ~5 s when history is mostly present
git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main   # now the real number (123 in our case)
```

After `--unshallow`, the repo is a normal full clone and `hermes update`'s
`is_shallow` branch no longer applies, so the problem self-heals for future runs.

items.title: [Bug]: sessions recover --allow-partial can exhaust its range-query budget and omit a recoverable tail row

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard
